title: Sonu Nigam Reveals He Was 'Banned' by T-Series and Zee Music Over Royalties Fight
excerpt: The veteran playback singer says India's two biggest music labels shut him out after he championed copyright and royalty rights for singers, a battle he says he chose at the peak of his career.
body:
• Sonu Nigam says T-Series and Zee Music Company both banned him after he publicly fought for singer royalties and copyright protections.
  • T-Series re-recorded his songs with other singers, including tracks in films like Main Tera Hero and Kick, after the dispute began around 2013.
  • Zee Music separately refused to work with Nigam, calling it a "business decision," and announced it would dub over his existing recordings.
  • Nigam's fight helped establish the Indian Singers Rights Association (ISRA) and contributed to fairer standard contracts across the industry.

Sonu Nigam, one of Bollywood's most celebrated playback singers, has revealed that he was effectively blacklisted by India's two largest music labels — T-Series and Zee Music Company — after he took up the fight for singers' royalty and copyright rights.

In a recent interview, Nigam described the professional fallout from his years-long advocacy as devastating. "Things only kept getting worse," the singer said, recalling how both labels systematically froze him out of the industry at what he described as the height of his career.

"God told me, 'You will leave your career at its peak. And you will take on this fight. If you don't do it, no one else will have the guts.'"

— Sonu Nigam

The T-Series Fallout

The dispute with T-Series, India's largest music label and the world's most-subscribed YouTube channel, traces back to around 2013. Nigam publicly demanded that T-Series pay royalties to singers for their recorded performances — a right that had been enshrined in India's Copyright Amendment Act of 2012 but was largely ignored by labels.

https://x.com/CNNnews18/status/2083793196941975871

T-Series chief Bhushan Kumar's response was swift and punishing. Songs already recorded by Nigam were re-dubbed with other singers' voices. His tracks in films including Main Tera Hero, Kick, and Heropanti were replaced. For a singer whose voice had defined Bollywood soundtracks for two decades, it amounted to professional erasure.

"If you are fighting for a cause, this is bound to happen," Nigam told Radio and Music at the time. "I did not compromise my principles and I faced everything that came."

The two sides eventually reconciled, with Kumar calling the rift "a miscommunication created by outsiders over the copyright issue" and describing Nigam as "my phenomenally talented younger brother." But the damage to Nigam's career during the freeze was real — the singer has said it felt like reliving his early struggling days.

Zee Music's Separate Ban

Even as T-Series tensions eased, Zee Music Company opened a separate front. The label announced it would not acquire any songs featuring Nigam and would re-record his existing tracks with other voices. The company framed the decision in corporate language, stating that "choosing not to work with any talent is based on business decision only."

The Zee dispute had its own triggers — Nigam had publicly criticized Zee News coverage in a separate incident — but the timing, coming on the heels of the T-Series royalty fight, reinforced the perception that speaking out against industry practices came at a steep price. Fans rallied behind the singer with the hashtag #IStandWithSonuNigam, which trended across social media.

A Bigger Battle Over Singers' Rights

Nigam's fight was never purely personal. India's Copyright Amendment Act of 2012 had granted performers — singers, musicians, and actors — the right to receive royalties for commercial use of their work. But implementation lagged for years. Music labels continued operating under legacy contracts that gave them near-total ownership of recordings, with singers receiving one-time session fees and nothing more.

Nigam became the most prominent voice calling for enforcement. He helped establish the Indian Singers Rights Association (ISRA), a collecting society that manages royalty distribution for vocalists. The organization was born out of a recognition that individual singers had no leverage against labels controlling the vast majority of Bollywood music distribution.

"In India, if you take a stand, instead of supporting you, they isolate you. When Taylor Swift took a stand against Spotify, people supported her. But in India, I was left out."

— Sonu Nigam

The contrast with how similar disputes played out in Western markets is telling. When Taylor Swift pulled her catalogue from Spotify in 2014 or publicly battled her former label over master recordings, the industry and public largely backed her. Nigam's experience in India was the opposite — industry peers stayed quiet while labels retaliated.

The Diaspora Connection

For the millions of Indian-origin music fans globally who grew up on Nigam's voice in tracks like "Kal Ho Naa Ho," "Abhi Mujh Mein Kahin," and "Suraj Hua Maddham," the revelation underscores a persistent gap in how India's entertainment industry treats its creative talent compared to global standards.

Where Things Stand Now

The landscape has shifted since Nigam's early battles. Standard contracts at T-Series, Sony Music India, and Zee Music now include royalty provisions, a change Nigam's advocacy helped bring about. ISRA continues to grow as a collecting body, and the broader copyright environment in India is evolving — Zee Entertainment has itself become an aggressive enforcer of its own music rights, recently suing both Nykaa and the Reliance-Disney venture JioStar over unauthorized use of its catalogue.

But Nigam's account, shared more than a decade after the worst of the backlash, serves as a reminder that the progress came at significant personal cost to the artists who pushed for it. The singer, now in his fifties, has described the period as one where he questioned whether his career could survive the stand he had taken.

"I will not do something that is illegal," Nigam has said. "Eventually good sense will prevail." For Indian singers still navigating an industry where labels hold outsized power, that good sense is still a work in progress.
